Use the menu to read the executive summary, findings, risk register, policies and detections.

docs.title: About this Hub
docs.text:
Fictional training data

Aura Workforce is a fictional company created for a security training programme. All people, accounts, salaries, bank numbers and incidents on this site are invented. Nothing here describes a real organisation or a real person.

docs.title: What this Hub shows
docs.text: This Hub lets a reader review the security work for Aura Workforce: findings, a risk register, policies and detection rules. It is built so that a client or auditor can check the evidence without touching anything dangerous.

docs.title: What is not published
docs.text:
• The vulnerable practice lab. It runs only on a private machine and is never hosted online.
  • Passwords, keys, tokens or any .env content.
  • Step-by-step exploit instructions that would work against real systems.
  • Real names, real email addresses or real personal data.

docs.title: Review of the content
docs.text: Pages are checked with a link checker and a spell check before each release.

docs.title: Detections
docs.text:
Fictional training data

The log data behind these rules is invented for a training project about a fictional company, Aura Workforce. Exact alert thresholds are deliberately not published.

Twelve detection rules were written and tested against three sets of logs: sign-in events, payroll audit events and web access logs. Every planted test event in the data was found.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule What it detects First checks for the responder A1 Brute force: repeated failed logins on one account Did a success follow the failures (see A5)? Lock the account and reset the password. A2 Password spraying: one address failing on many accounts Block the address. Check whether any of those accounts later had a success from it. A3 Impossible travel: logins from two countries too close together in time Call the user. Was MFA used on the second login? Kill sessions and reset the password. A4 Successful login outside working hours (one alert per user per night) Was MFA used? Is the address known for this user? Ask the user or manager and check what they did after logging in. A5 Success from an address that had many earlier failures Treat the account as compromised: disable it and review its actions since the login. P1 Full payroll export Who ran it, when, and was there a ticket? Check where the file went. P2 Salary change with no approval Reverse the change, find the approver, and check with HR whether it was legitimate. P3 Burst of salary views by one person Compare with this user's normal behaviour, ask the manager, and check which employees were viewed. W1 SQL injection, cross-site scripting or path traversal patterns in web requests Check the status code (200 or 500 means it reached the app), review the app logs, and block the address. W2 Web login brute force Block the address, check for a success after the rejections, and review the targeted account. W3 Scanning: many "not found" responses from one address Block the address and check whether any probe returned a real page. W4 Probing for sensitive paths (admin pages, configuration files, source folders, backups) Check whether any request succeeded and whether the file really exists.

docs.title: How the rules were tuned
docs.text:
Thresholds were set from the busiest normal activity in the same logs, with headroom, so normal behaviour does not raise alerts. Exact values are kept private, because published numbers tell an attacker how much activity stays under the alert.

Rule A4 groups logins into one alert per user per night, so a single incident is one alert and not several.

docs.title: Handling a legitimate exception
docs.text:
Suppose a trusted administrator really does log in at an unusual hour for a scheduled job. The rule is not switched off. Instead:

  • A narrow exception is added that matches only when the user, source, country and time window all fit. A login that differs on any of these still alerts.
  • The account requires MFA.
  • A dedicated account is used for that job and for nothing else, and an alert fires if it does anything other than the job.

docs.title: Where this connects
docs.text: Each rule links to a playbook in the incident response policy and to a threat in the policies page, so an alert always has a defined next step.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Fictional training data

Aura Workforce is a fictional company. Everything below comes from a training project, and no real organisation or person is described.

docs.title: What was done
docs.text:
A security review was carried out for Aura Workforce, a payroll and HR platform that holds pay, ratings and personal details. The work covered:

  • Risk assessment: 22 risks scored and ranked, each with an owner and a due date.
  • Testing: a private practice lab and a passive scan, with every alert checked by hand.
  • Policies: 10 policies and 90 rules, each with an auditor check and a linked threat.
  • Detection: 12 rules that find attacks in sign-in, payroll and web logs.

docs.title: Where things stand
docs.text: The register holds 8 Critical, 11 High and 3 Medium risks. None is closed yet: fixes count only once they are built and tested on the real application, not only on the practice lab.

docs.title: Most urgent
docs.text:
Five risks tie at the top score, so they were ranked by evidence of real misuse, then by speed of fix:

  1. Leavers and shared accounts still active. Disable them and close accounts automatically on the exit date.
  2. No multi-factor authentication on admin, HR, payroll and finance accounts.
  3. Brute-force password guessing. Add lockout, a longer minimum length and a breached-password check.
  4. SQL injection. Use safe queries everywhere.
  5. Employees reading each other's salaries by changing an ID. The server must check ownership on every request.

docs.title: Main lesson
docs.text: An automated scan with no High results does not mean a system is safe. The most serious problems came from manual testing, so both are needed, and every alert must be checked before it is reported.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• Findings: what was wrong, how serious, and the fix.
  • Risk register: the top five and how ties were ranked.
  • Policies: the policy index, one full example and the threat-to-rule map.
  • Detections: what each rule detects and what the responder checks first.
  • About this Hub: what is and is not published.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Fictional training data

These findings come from a deliberately vulnerable practice web app, run privately on one machine. It stands in for the Aura Workforce application. No real system was tested, and no exploit steps are published here.

docs.title: How the findings were produced
docs.text: An automated passive scan (ZAP baseline) was run first. Every alert was then checked by hand, and the results were compared with earlier manual testing. A finding is marked Real only after it was reproduced.

docs.title: Verified findings, ranked by severity
docs.text: # Finding Verdict Severity Fix 1 Script runs from the search box (DOM-based XSS) Real, confirmed by hand. The scanner rated it Low from a code pattern only. High Never pass user input into trusted-HTML functions. Sanitise or escape it. Add a Content Security Policy. 2 Internal files readable without login Real, missed by the scanner High Remove the public route, keep files outside the web root, require login. 3 Content Security Policy header missing Real Medium Add the header, starting in report-only mode. 4 Detailed error page leaks internal information Real, missed by the scanner Low Show a generic error page. Keep traces in server logs only. 5 Cross-origin access allowed for every site Real, low impact Low Restrict to the app's own origin. 6 Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header missing Real, hardening only Low Add the header and test that embeds still work. 7 Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header missing Real, hardening only Low Add the header. 8 Deprecated browser-feature header in use Real, trivial Info Replace it with the current Permissions-Policy header. 9 Cache alerts and "modern web application" note Not vulnerabilities, or false alarms Info None.

docs.title: Rating notes
docs.text:
• Finding 1 is High because it needs no login, works from one crafted link, and runs script in the victim's browser.
  • Finding 2 is rated High, not Critical: the most sensitive file was an encrypted vault, but downloading it still allows unlimited offline guessing, and another file was readable in plain text. The rating would go up if the vault password were weak.

docs.title: Other issues found by manual testing
docs.text:
These were found by hand because a passive scan cannot see them. Details are kept private.

  • One user could read another user's shopping basket by changing an ID (broken access control).
  • Login could be bypassed with crafted input (SQL injection).
  • A login token contained a password hash.
  • Several old software dependencies were in use.
  • The password reset question was weak, which allowed account takeover.
  • There was no account lockout after repeated wrong passwords.
  • A shopping basket accepted a negative quantity (business-logic flaw).
  • Too little logging existed to trace these actions.

Each of these is tracked in the risk register with an owner and a due date.

docs.title: Status after the remediation sprint
docs.text: The matching register risks for access control (R-01), login bypass (R-02) and missing lockout (R-04) were fixed or reduced in lab copies and tested again. The other items above are still open. See the remediation status for what each fix proved and what is still open.

docs.title: Scanner versus manual testing
docs.text:
Where the scanner helped Where the scanner failed Fast check of headers and configuration Wrongly passed several checks that were real (open internal files, detailed errors, server-side old packages) Found missing security headers and the cross-origin setting Cannot log in, so it misses access control, injection, authentication and business-logic flaws Cheap to repeat on every build Also produced noise: junk URLs and cache alerts

Lesson: a scan with no High results does not mean a system is safe. The most serious items came from manual testing. Use both, and check every alert before reporting it.

Free-tier terms were checked on 18 November 2026. They change often, so check the provider's pricing page before relying on any figure.

docs.title: Choice for this Hub
docs.text: A documentation site is a few hundred kilobytes of static files with no secrets, so free static hosting is enough. A paid server would add a machine to defend for no gain.

docs.title: Monitoring evidence
docs.text: The detection rules were run as scripts on sample logs. No live monitoring stack runs behind this Hub, because the project did not need one. Evidence is shown as rule descriptions and test results, and the scripts are kept in a private repository. A real deployment would run monitoring on a small paid server.

docs.title: The vulnerable lab stays private
docs.text: The practice lab runs only on a private machine, bound to the local address. It is never hosted, and the Hub repository does not contain it.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
Fictional training data

These policies were written for a fictional company, Aura Workforce. Roles, dates and figures are invented for a training project.

The policy pack has 10 policies and 90 rules. Every rule has an auditor check (how someone can prove it is followed) and a linked threat (why the rule exists).

docs.title: Policy index
docs.text: No. Policy Rules 01 Access Control and Least Privilege AC-01 to AC-09 02 Passwords and MFA PW-01 to PW-09 03 Data Classification and Handling DC-01 to DC-09 04 Encryption EN-01 to EN-09 05 Logging and Monitoring LM-01 to LM-09 06 Incident Response IR-01 to IR-09 07 Backup and Recovery BR-01 to BR-09 08 Secure Development SD-01 to SD-09 09 Third Parties and Cloud TP-01 to TP-09 10 Acceptable Use and Awareness AU-01 to AU-09

docs.title: Example: Policy 01, Access Control and Least Privilege
docs.text: Owner Security Lead Version 1.0 Effective 21 October 2026 Review date 21 October 2027

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: People and systems get only the access they need for their job, and nothing more. This protects Restricted and Confidential data such as pay, ratings and personal details.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: All Aura Workforce staff, contractors, user accounts, service accounts, the web app, the API, the payroll engine, the ledger, the dashboards and the database.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: ID Rule How an auditor checks it Threat AC-01 Every account belongs to one named person or one named service. Shared accounts such as "admin" or "payroll" are not allowed. Export the user list: every username maps to an employee ID or a service owner. T-16 AC-02 Access is given by role. The roles and what each may see are written in an access matrix approved by the data owner. The access matrix exists with approver and date. Check 5 users: their rights match the matrix. T-06 AC-03 The server checks the user's role and ownership on every request. Hiding a button or menu is not enough. Log in as an employee and request another employee's payslip in 10 tests. All 10 return "access denied". T-06, T-07, T-28 AC-04 Only the Payroll role can start a payroll run, and a second person approves it. The logs of the last 3 payroll runs show two different user IDs for each run. T-12 AC-05 Restricted columns (pay, ratings, date of birth, leave reason) can be read only by the roles named in the data classification worksheet. Compare database permissions with the "who should access it" column of the worksheet. No extra roles have access. T-06, T-07 AC-06 The API, payroll engine and ledger each use their own database account with only the permissions they need. No application uses an admin database account. List the database accounts: there is one per service and none has admin rights. T-10, T-20 AC-07 A dashboard shows a group only if it has at least 5 people. Open a dashboard for a team of 2 people: it shows "not enough data". T-27 AC-08 The account of a person who leaves is disabled within 1 working day of the exit date. Compare HR exit dates with account disable dates for the last 10 leavers: all within 1 working day. T-01 AC-09 Data owners review who has access every 90 days and sign the result. Signed review records exist for the last 2 quarters. T-07

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
• Data owner (HR head for HR data, Finance head for ledger data): approves the access matrix and does the 90-day review.
  • Security Lead: keeps this policy, approves exceptions, checks the evidence.
  • System administrator: creates and removes accounts as the access matrix says.
  • Line manager: requests access for their team and tells HR when someone leaves.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: Only the Security Lead may approve an exception, in writing. An exception lasts at most 30 days, is recorded in the exception register, and ends automatically on its date. Emergency ("break glass") access is logged and reviewed within 1 working day.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: This policy is reviewed once a year, or after a security incident that involves access.

docs.title: Why each rule exists: top 10 threats mapped to rules
docs.text: Rank Threat Rules that reduce it How the rules work together 1 T-06 Employee reads a colleague's payslip by changing the employee ID AC-02, AC-03, AC-05, SD-03, SD-08, LM-02, LM-08, AU-04 The server checks ownership (AC-03, SD-03) and tests prove it on every build (SD-08). Logs and alerts (LM-02, LM-08) catch any miss, and AU-04 makes snooping misconduct. 2 T-09 SQL injection on API to Database SD-02, SD-07, SD-08, EN-06, PW-04, IR-04 Safe queries stop it (SD-02). Scans catch gaps (SD-07, SD-08). If it still happens, encrypted Restricted columns and hashed passwords limit the damage (EN-06, PW-04), and containment starts within 1 hour (IR-04). 3 T-01 Stolen or guessed password used to log in PW-01, PW-02, PW-03, PW-05, LM-01, LM-07, IR-05, AU-05, AU-06 MFA, long passwords and lockout make guessing fail. Alerts show attacks (LM-07). A compromised account is disabled within 1 hour (IR-05). Training and phishing tests reduce theft (AU-05, AU-06). 4 T-27 Dashboard for a very small team reveals one person's pay or rating AC-07, DC-02, AU-04 A dashboard hides groups under 5 people (AC-07). The data owner reviews classification every 6 months (DC-02). Misuse is misconduct and alerts are investigated (AU-04). 5 T-10 One powerful database account used by the API AC-06, DC-01, TP-04, TP-05, AU-09 Each service has its own limited account (AC-06). Columns have levels (DC-01). Cloud databases are never public (TP-04) and cloud admins use MFA (TP-05). Administrators are trained (AU-09). 6 T-07 Employee sends a request that changes a salary figure AC-03, AC-05, AC-09, SD-01, SD-03, SD-04, LM-03 Server-side role checks and input checks block it (AC-03, SD-03, SD-04). A second person reviews code (SD-01). Every change to salary data is logged with old and new value (LM-03). Access is reviewed every 90 days (AC-09). 7 T-12 Non-payroll user starts a payroll run AC-04, SD-03, LM-05 Only the Payroll role can start a run and a second person approves it (AC-04). Endpoint tests prove the check (SD-03). Each run records who started and approved it (LM-05). 8 T-14 Payroll rows edited after the run LM-03, SD-01, BR-02, BR-08, IR-04, IR-06 Changes are logged (LM-03) and code changes are reviewed (SD-01). Point-in-time backups let the team compare and undo (BR-02, BR-08). Evidence is kept and containment is fast (IR-06, IR-04). 9 T-05 Stolen or forged session token used on the API PW-07, EN-09, IR-05, AU-05, AU-06 Short sessions and logout cancel tokens (PW-07). Tokens are signed, so a changed one is rejected (EN-09). A compromised account is cut off within 1 hour (IR-05). Training reduces theft (AU-05, AU-06). 10 T-32 Ransomware locks the database BR-01, BR-03, BR-06, BR-07, BR-09, IR-01, IR-08, LM-09, SD-07, TP-08 Daily backups with an offline copy (BR-01, BR-03) are tested every quarter (BR-06). Recovery targets and an offline plan make recovery fast (BR-07, BR-09). A response plan and a payroll fallback keep staff paid (IR-01, IR-08). Alerts, patching and supplier checks reduce the chance (LM-09, SD-07, TP-08).

docs.title: Risk register
docs.text:
Fictional training data

All figures, accounts and incidents on this page are invented for a training project about a fictional company, Aura Workforce.

The register holds 22 risks: 8 Critical, 11 High and 3 Medium. Each risk is scored likelihood x impact (1 to 5 each, maximum 25). Five risks tie at a score of 20, so the order below uses a tie-break rule.

docs.title: Top five risks
docs.text: Order Risk (score) Why it matters Fix Owner Due 1st R-19 Leavers and shared accounts (20) 6 leavers still active (one logged in 157 days after exit), 2 shared accounts, 5 dormant accounts Disable them now. Close accounts automatically on the HR exit date (AC-08). IT manager 20 Nov 2026 2nd R-17 No MFA (20) 5 admins and 18 Finance or HR accounts have no MFA. Detection rule A4 saw a login without it. Turn on MFA for every Admin, HR, Payroll and Finance account (PW-01). Security Lead 27 Nov 2026 3rd R-04 Brute force (20) 420 failed logins on one account, then a success Lockout after 5 wrong tries (PW-05), 12-character minimum, breached-password check Development lead 27 Nov 2026 4th R-02 SQL injection (20) Gives admin access with no password. Attempts reached the app in the log review. Parameterised queries everywhere, scan with 0 injection findings, encrypt Restricted columns Development lead 27 Nov 2026 5th R-01 IDOR (20) Any employee can read a colleague's salary by changing an ID. Proven in the practice lab. Server checks ownership on every request. 10 "access denied" tests pass on every build. Development lead 27 Nov 2026

docs.title: Remediation status (19 November 2026)
docs.text:
The five top risks were fixed in lab copies. Each fix was then tested again with the same check used before it. Scores are unchanged: they drop only after the fix is built and tested on Aura Workforce itself.

Risk Status Result of the retest Still open R-19 Leavers and shared accounts Fixed in lab copy, retest passed The access review was rerun on a copy of the data. Leaver, shared and dormant accounts went from 13 to 0. Named replacement accounts still have to be created. Not yet done on Aura. R-17 No MFA Process proven only, retest passed on a copy MFA gaps on Admin, HR and Finance accounts went from 23 to 0 in the review copy. Enrolment was simulated. MFA is not enforced on Aura yet. Most other accounts still have no MFA. R-04 Brute force Partly mitigated Repeated wrong passwords at the practice login are now refused by a rate limit in front of the lab, and the limit clears after a short wait. The limit is per address, not per account. The policy asks for a per-account lockout. R-02 SQL injection Fixed in lab copy, retest passed A crafted login that got in before the fix is refused after it. Proven on one route. The code scan is the wider evidence. Not yet on Aura. R-01 IDOR Fixed in lab copy, retest passed Reading a colleague's payslip was allowed before and is refused after, unless the person is the owner or HR. HR keeps the access its job needs. Not yet on Aura.

docs.title: Regression checklist
docs.text:
Run before every release. A release is blocked if any check fails.

  1. A crafted login attempt is refused with a plain failure and no database error text.
  2. Code scans show no injection findings, and all database queries use safe parameters.
  3. Payslip pages need a login.
  4. An employee cannot open another employee's payslip, and can still open their own.
  5. HR can still open any payslip.
  6. Admins cannot open other people's payslips, as the access matrix says.
  7. Repeated wrong passwords are refused at the login.
  8. The refusal clears after a short wait, so nobody is locked out for good.
  9. The monthly access review shows no active leaver, shared or dormant accounts.
  10. The monthly access review shows MFA on every Admin, HR, Payroll and Finance account.

docs.title: How five risks with the same score were ranked
docs.text:
1. Proof first: a risk with real evidence of misuse (an actual login or a successful attack) comes first. A risk with only failed attempts or lab evidence comes later.
  2. Quick fix first: if the proof is equal, the risk that can be fixed in hours goes before the one that takes weeks.
  3. Shared fix first: if the fix times are equal, the fix that also lowers other risks goes first.
  4. Impact last: if everything above is equal, the higher impact goes first.

docs.title: What would change each rating
docs.text: Risk What would LOWER it What would RAISE it R-19 The 13 old accounts are disabled and accounts close automatically on the exit date. Score 4 to 8. Logs show a leaver or shared account touching Restricted data. Score 25. R-17 A new review shows MFA on 100% of Admin, HR, Payroll and Finance accounts. Score 5 to 10. Rule A4 shows an off-hours login with no MFA on a payroll account from an unknown address. Score 25. R-04 Lockout is built and tested, and MFA is on targeted accounts. Score 8. The attacked account is an admin or payroll account with no MFA. Score 25. R-02 Safe queries everywhere, 0 scan findings, Restricted columns encrypted. Score 8. Rule W1 shows an injection attempt that reached the app with status 200 or 500. Score 25. R-01 Ownership check on every request, 10 "access denied" tests pass on every build. Score 10. A log shows a real request using another employee's ID and getting a 200. Score 25.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Fixes count only once they are built and tested on Aura Workforce itself, not only on the practice lab apps.
  • R-04 and R-17 come from the same event (one admin account with no MFA, hit by 420 failed logins). One fix, MFA, lowers both.
  • R-01 was the number-one threat in the threat model. It is ranked fifth only because the logs show no attack on Aura yet. It did not become less serious.
  • This register is a learning exercise. It is not legal advice.
